transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Yeah, thanks for fitting me in. Well, it’s kind of a long story, but I guess the main thing that brings me in today is... well, I just feel like I’m always moving from one thing to the next. Like, I literally can’t just idle. It’s like a car engine that's just left running in the driveway, you know? 

I’ve been a customer service rep for a long time, and for years I sort of had my own little ways of dealing with it—pacing on the phone, shuffling my papers around, just keeping in motion. I've always been that way, just needing to do something. But lately, we had this whole restructuring at work. They changed the floor plan, put in this new open-desk arrangement, and honestly, the new work setup has made that a lot harder to hide. I used to be able to just quietly keep moving in my own space, but now everyone can see everything, and I feel like I stick out like a sore thumb because I just can't stay put. I'm always shifting, always onto the next thing, and it's just... it's getting exhausting trying to pretend I can just sit quietly at a desk for eight hours when I just physically can't seem to idle. So, I figured I should finally come talk to someone about it.
Outside of work, do you find yourself struggling to stay focused or sitting still, or do you often feel restless or impulsive in other parts of your life, like at home or during social activities?

Oh, absolutely. It’s funny you bring up home, because my wife actually mentions this all the time. You know, you get home from a long day on the phones—and like I said, customer service is draining, especially with that new open floor plan where everybody's right on top of you—so you’d think I’d just want to crash, right? Just sink into my recliner and do absolutely nothing. And I try, I really do try to just do the quiet stuff that’s supposed to relax me. 

Like, my wife loves to put on a movie in the evenings, usually one of those long historical dramas or mysteries she likes, or I’ll try to sit down with a book. I’ve got this whole stack of paperbacks by the nightstand I’ve been meaning to get through for months. But... well, it just doesn’t last long. I mean, we’ll be sitting there, and I’ll give it maybe fifteen, twenty minutes, and then I’m just shifting around in the chair, trying to get comfortable, crossing one leg, then the other. And then I start commenting on the movie—you know, pointing out things that don't make sense or asking where I've seen that one actor before, which drives her absolutely up the wall because she actually wants to hear the dialogue, bless her heart. 

And if I'm not doing that, I'm getting up for something. I’ll tell her I need to get a glass of water, or I need to go check if the back porch light is off, or I just remember I need to take the recycling out right that second. It’s like, even when I'm supposed to be relaxing and enjoying a quiet night in, I just can't stay anchored to the couch. I just... I don't know, sitting through a whole movie or just reading quietly, it just doesn't happen without me shifting around or having to get up and do *something*.
Do you often find it hard to focus on tasks or conversations, feel easily distracted, or have trouble finishing things you start, even if they’re important?

Well, yeah, that’s another thing that’s really been getting under my skin lately, especially with work. You see, being a customer service rep, we have these coaching meetings. And they used to be pretty quick, you know, just a quick huddle, 'here's what we're doing today, go get 'em.' But since the whole restructuring thing I mentioned, management has decided we need these longer, drawn-out coaching sessions. And they hand out these new procedure manuals—thick packets, stapled together, full of all this corporate jargon about 'synergy' and 'customer retention strategies' and all that. 

And I really try, I mean I sit there in the meeting room—which is freezing, by the way, I don't know why they always keep those conference rooms so cold—and I tell myself, 'Okay, pay attention, this is important.' And I start off fine! I’m looking right at the supervisor, nodding along, or I’m looking at the first paragraph of the new procedure. But then... I don't know, it’s like my brain just takes a detour. I’ll be staring right at the paper, and after a few minutes, I’ll suddenly realize that my eyes have been moving down the page, like I'm reading, but I haven't actually taken in a single word. Or the supervisor will be talking, and I’ll realize I’ve been thinking about whether I need to get the oil changed in the Honda, or if I remembered to put the trash bins on the curb. And then I have to sort of scramble mentally to figure out what they just said, because I know they were talking, I heard the noise, but the actual meaning just completely bypassed me. It’s so frustrating because I *want* to focus, I really do, but it’s like my attention span just has a mind of its own and decides to clock out after five minutes.
Do you often feel a strong urge to speak or act without thinking, or find yourself interrupting others during conversations or activities more than you'd like?

Yeah, actually, that’s... well, it’s funny you mention that, because that’s another huge issue that has really come to a head with this new open floor plan I was telling you about earlier. Before the restructuring, we had those traditional cubicles, you know, with the high gray fabric walls where you could kind of just tune out the rest of the world. You couldn't really hear what the person next to you was saying unless they were practically yelling. But now, they’ve got us sitting at these low-profile pods. It's basically four desks pushed together with absolutely no dividers. Management calls it a "collaborative environment," but really, it just means I can hear every single word of everyone else's phone calls all day long.

And the thing is, I’ve been a rep for a long time. I know our computer system inside and out, backwards and forwards. I know all the workarounds. So if I’m sitting there—maybe I’m in between calls or just doing some wrap-up data entry—and I hear one of my coworkers working through a customer problem... I just, I can't seem to stop myself. Like, there's this younger guy, Kevin, who sits right across from me. Nice kid, but he's still learning the ropes. If I hear him on his headset trying to figure out why a refund hasn't processed or why a shipping address isn't validating, I don’t mean to be rude, I really don't, but I’ll just jump right in with the answer before he’s even finished his sentence to the customer, or before anyone has even asked me for help. 

I'll just blurt it out right across the desk. I'll be like, "Kevin, it's the billing zip code, you have to bypass the secondary screen!" And it just comes flying out of my mouth before I even realize I'm speaking. It’s like the answer is right there in my head and there's this physical pressure to just get it out and solve the problem immediately. Then Kevin gets all flustered, and the customer gets confused because they can hear me shouting in the background, and my supervisor gives me *that* look. I know I shouldn't do it, and I tell myself every morning to just mind my own business, but the second I hear someone stuck on a problem, the words just bypass my brain and come right out. I do it at home, too, you know, finishing my wife's sentences for her, but at work, it's just becoming a real sticking point because I'm basically stepping all over everyone else's calls.
Do you ever feel nervous, anxious, or on edge for no clear reason, even when things are going fine?

Well, no, not really. I mean, if things are actually going fine, then I'm fine. I don't just get that... that feeling of dread or whatever you'd call it out of nowhere. 

Don't get me wrong, I get stressed, but there is always a very clear, very loud reason for it. Like with work, or Kevin, or the new call metrics management wants us to hit. But just sitting around on a Sunday when there's nothing going on? No, I'm not nervous. I might be bored, and like I said, I can't sit still for the life of me, but I'm not anxious. 

Like last weekend, I was out in the driveway washing the Honda—finally got around to it, it was completely covered in pollen, just a yellow mess all over the windshield—and it was a beautiful afternoon. I'm out there with the bucket and the sponge, just scrubbing away at the hubcaps. And I'm perfectly content! I'm not standing there worrying about the sky falling or anything like that. Now, if the hose gets kinked—and it always does, right when you've got the soap on the roof and it starts drying in the sun, leaving those awful white water spots—sure, I'll get a little wound up and frustrated. But that's a reaction to something actually happening right in front of me. 

Or if my supervisor is pacing behind my pod with his clipboard, yeah, I'm on edge then, because I know he's listening to my call times. But just out of the blue, for absolutely no reason at all? No, I don't really experience that. My wife, bless her, she can be a bit of a worrier, always fretting about whether she left the coffee pot on or if our daughter's car needs new tires, but me? If there's no fire, I'm not worried about the smoke, you know? I just don't get worked up unless there's a specific problem staring me in the face.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy lately?

Well, no, not at all. I mean, sure, I get irritated with the whole open-floor plan thing and the new metrics they're pushing at work, but down? Hopeless? No, definitely not. I still get a real kick out of the things I’ve always enjoyed. 

Like, I was just telling you about washing the Honda earlier. Well, after I washed it, I actually spent another two hours putting a fresh coat of wax on it. And I don't use that cheap liquid spray stuff they sell now where you just wipe it on and off, either. I use the real carnauba paste wax, the kind that comes in the little tin. You have to apply it in these tight little circles, let it haze over just the right amount—if you leave it in the sun too long it turns into absolute concrete, let me tell you, and you'll pull a muscle trying to get it off—and then you buff it out by hand with a clean microfiber cloth. It takes a lot of elbow grease, especially on my shoulders at my age, but I really enjoy it. I get a ton of satisfaction out of stepping back and seeing that mirror shine on the hood. If I was losing interest in things, I certainly wouldn't be out there sweating over a 2014 Accord for three hours on a Sunday! 

And my wife and I still do our Friday night bowling league, too. We’ve been going to the same alley for, oh, it has to be fifteen years now. We always try to get lane 14, and we always get a basket of those terrible, greasy crinkle-cut fries they make at the snack bar. I look forward to it every single week. My average has dropped a bit lately, probably because I keep looking up at the TVs over the lanes to check the baseball scores when I should be looking at the arrows, but I still have a great time. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel sad or empty or anything like that. My brain might be going a million miles a minute in the wrong direction half the time, and I can't sit through a coaching meeting to save my life, but my mood is generally pretty good!
Looking back on your childhood, did you notice that you had trouble sitting still, staying focused, or controlling impulses, or was this something that mostly started in adulthood?

Oh, no, no, this isn't a new thing at all. It’s definitely been around long, long before this whole open-floor plan mess or this job change. Actually, it’s funny you ask about my childhood, because when my mother passed a few years back, my sister and I were cleaning out her house—she lived in the same split-level for forty years, so you can imagine the amount of stuff we had to go through, just boxes and boxes of memories—and we found this old shoebox tucked way back in the hall closet. She had kept every single one of my report cards from grade school. Every single one! 

And I sat down on the floor right there in the hallway and started reading through them, and it was honestly like reading a review of my performance at the call center today. I mean, back then, we had those heavy wooden desks with the tops that lifted up, where you kept your Big Chief tablets and your pencils, and the teachers would write these detailed notes on the back of the report cards in that perfect cursive they all used to have. 

Year after year, from Mrs. Gable in second grade right on up to Mr. Henderson in fifth, they all wrote the exact same thing. They’d write that I was a bright boy, but that I was careless. Always that word, "careless." And they constantly noted that I talked out of turn—which, I guess, is exactly what I'm doing to poor Kevin now, just blurting out the answers before anyone else can speak! I'd know the answer to a history question or a math problem and I just couldn't keep my hand raised, I'd just shout it out. 

And the other thing they always, always wrote was that I had to be constantly reminded to stay with my work. I’d be supposed to be doing my spelling sentences, and instead I’d be lifting the desk lid up and down to see how the hinges worked, or watching the janitor mow the grass outside, and the teacher would have to walk down the aisle and tap my paper to get me back on track. My dad used to get so frustrated at the kitchen table trying to get me through my homework, too. So, yeah, I’ve been like this since I was in short pants. It’s not just the adult stress or the new management at work... it's just how I've always been.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced symptoms before age 12, which is a criterion for F90.0 (ADHD, Combined Presentation) and helps differentiate it from F32.0 (Major Depressive Disorder), which typically has a later onset.
doctor.question: Looking back on your childhood, did you notice that you had trouble sitting still, staying focused, or controlling impulses, or was this something that mostly started in adulthood?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Looking back, this was around long before this job change; in grade school my teachers wrote that I was bright but careless, talked out of turn, and had to be reminded to stay with my work.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity were present during childhood, which directly corresponds to the requirement of symptom onset prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
Oh, no, no, this isn't a new thing at all. It’s definitely been around long, long before this whole open-floor plan mess or this job change. Actually, it’s funny you ask about my childhood, because when my mother passed a few years back, my sister and I were cleaning out her house—she lived in the same split-level for forty years, so you can imagine the amount of stuff we had to go through, just boxes and boxes of memories—and we found this old shoebox tucked way back in the hall closet. She had kept every single one of my report cards from grade school. Every single one! 

And I sat down on the floor right there in the hallway and started reading through them, and it was honestly like reading a review of my performance at the call center today. I mean, back then, we had those heavy wooden desks with the tops that lifted up, where you kept your Big Chief tablets and your pencils, and the teachers would write these detailed notes on the back of the report cards in that perfect cursive they all used to have. 

Year after year, from Mrs. Gable in second grade right on up to Mr. Henderson in fifth, they all wrote the exact same thing. They’d write that I was a bright boy, but that I was careless. Always that word, "careless." And they constantly noted that I talked out of turn—which, I guess, is exactly what I'm doing to poor Kevin now, just blurting out the answers before anyone else can speak! I'd know the answer to a history question or a math problem and I just couldn't keep my hand raised, I'd just shout it out. 

And the other thing they always, always wrote was that I had to be constantly reminded to stay with my work. I’d be supposed to be doing my spelling sentences, and instead I’d be lifting the desk lid up and down to see how the hinges worked, or watching the janitor mow the grass outside, and the teacher would have to walk down the aisle and tap my paper to get me back on track. My dad used to get so frustrated at the kitchen table trying to get me through my homework, too. So, yeah, I’ve been like this since I was in short pants. It’s not just the adult stress or the new management at work... it's just how I've always been.

Symptoms are pervasive across settings (work, home, social), and the patient notes that these behaviors have been present since early childhood, as evidenced by report cards and family history.
